articles.title: ICC prosecution seeks admission of expert report, 3 witness testimonies
articles.summary: Prosecutors of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are asking judges to admit an expert report and the previously recorded testimonies of three witnesses into evidence in the crimes against…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 5:19am

Prosecutors of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are asking judges to admit an expert report and the previously recorded testimonies of three witnesses into evidence in the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte.

In two public redacted filings dated October 23, the Office of the Prosecutor asked Trial Chamber III to admit the materials under Rule 68(3) of the ICC’s Rules of Procedure and Evidence, while still allowing limited live questioning of the witnesses in court.
In the first document, the prosecution sought to introduce the expert report of witness P-1400 and 15 associated items for its fourth application under Rule 68(3)
The witness’s field of expertise, as well as much of the subject matter covered by the report, was redacted from the public filing.
Prosecutors said the report was relevant, reliable, and probative, and would help the Chamber determine the issues in the case.
They also asked for two hours to conduct a focused supplementary examination of P-1400, instead of an estimated five hours of direct examination.

“Granting the Request will enhance the expeditiousness of the proceedings by reducing the length of the witness’s direct examination from five hours to two hours, saving approximately three hours of court time,” the filing stated.
The prosecution said P-1400 would first adopt the expert report before being asked supplementary questions on matters requiring clarification or elaboration.

It said this would avoid having the witness repeat every issue already addressed in the written report while preserving the opportunity for the defense, victims’ lawyers and the judges to question the witness.

The prosecution also argued that admitting the report would not prejudice Duterte’s rights because his lawyers had agreed in principle to the introduction of expert reports under Rule 68(3) and would still be able to question P-1400.
Three witnesses on alleged murders

In a separate fifth Rule 68(3) application filing, prosecutors asked the Chamber to admit the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-1155, P-1156 and P-1157, together with associated materials. The three would still appear in court and remain available for questioning and cross-examination.
The prosecution said their evidence relates to alleged murders charged under Count 3, although the particular incident and several details remain redacted.

Prosecutors said P-1155 and P-1156 provide direct evidence on the killings and on Duterte’s alleged knowledge and intent, while the three witnesses also give evidence concerning the alleged policy to “neutralize” suspected criminals through violent crimes.
Prosecutors said P-1155’s statement covers, among other matters, alleged orders “from above,” police instructions and a reward linked to the incident.
P-1156’s account concerns alleged orders, planning, preparations and payment, while P-1157 provides evidence on a killing and a planned police operation against the targets.
Much of the surrounding detail in the three witnesses’ testimonies remains redacted.

The prosecution said the three testimonies are “internally consistent” and mutually corroborative, and argued that admitting them would not prejudice Duterte because his lawyers would still be able to cross-examine the witnesses in court.

The filings come ahead of the final status conference scheduled for November 2, where the Chamber is expected to address remaining trial-preparation concerns before proceedings open for Duterte’s case on November 30.
The ICC has said the Chamber will resolve pending matters and adopt procedures needed for the fair and expeditious conduct of the trial before it begins.
Trial Chamber III, composed of Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou, has yet to rule on the two prosecution requests. — VBL, GMA News

blocks.text: Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the Health Ministry said on Friday.
Officials said the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.
"Sadly, she succumbed to ⁠the ​disease early ​this evening," the ministry said.
Seven people continue to receive treatment for the illness in Kenya.
What else do we know about the 2nd Kenyan Ebola death?
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago. She began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
Medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life," the ministry said, adding that it had notified her family and would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
Kenya's first Ebola case was announced on October 6. A 40-year-old Kenyan man living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3.
He tested positive for the disease on October 5 and died on the same day.
Of some 135 who were identified as contacts with the patient, 118 were placed in quarantine, with eight testing positive. They included four health workers and four close family members.
The latest death is believed to have been among those quarantined family members. The ministry said she developed symptoms on October 13.
The remaining seven cases are all within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry added.

articles.title: Google Maps changed its default voice to be more 'natural.' People hate it
articles.summary: The new voice for the directions feature on Google Maps started rolling out earlier this year as part of the tech giant's ongoing updates to improve the driving experience and make voice guidance…

image.caption: The new voice giving directions on Google Maps is part of the app's 'biggest navigation upgrade in over a decade,' Google said earlier this year. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The new voice for the directions feature on Google Maps started rolling out earlier this year as part of the tech giant's ongoing updates to improve the driving experience and make voice guidance more natural with help from its Gemini chatbot models.
New voice for directions began rolling out earlier this year, tech giant confirms
It's been described as "angry and unfriendly," "an entitled know-it-all" and akin to "a snarky barista who wants to tell you how to live your life."

Google Maps has changed its default voice for directions — you know, the one that tells you where to turn and how many kilometres until the off-ramp — and it's safe to say many people are not fans of the new mouthpiece directing them from Point A to Point B.
"Why does my Google Maps default voice suddenly sound like a Mid-Western white woman?" someone wrote on X on Friday.
"The vocal fry kills me," a person commented on Reddit.
"I want directions to my next business meeting, not an effing latte," someone said in the Google Maps support forum.

In a statement to CBC News, Google explained the new voice started rolling out earlier this year as part of its ongoing updates to improve the driving experience and make voice guidance more natural with help from Gemini models.

items: Time for a digital divorce? Trade war puts spotlight on Canada's relationship with U.S. big tech

blocks.text: Google started incorporating Gemini, its artificial intelligence chatbot, into its mapping applications in 2024.

There doesn't appear to be a formal announcement about the voice change on the company's website, other than a line within a larger March 2026 blog post saying it had "updated voice guidance to be more natural, like a friend navigating with you."
If the criticisms online are any indication, a lot people don't exactly think the new voice is friendly.
"She sounds like someone who wouldn't like me," someone wrote on X this week.
"Sounds kind of annoyed it has to give you directions," another person wrote on Reddit.
Lake Ontario reinstated on Google Maps for Canadian websites
People generally don't like voice changes

Google launched Maps in 2005 as a desktop application advertised as a new solution to help people "get from point A to point B," the company explains in a blog post. It went mobile in 2007 (on Blackberry, followed by Android in 2008 and iOS in 2012) and added turn-by-turn instructions in 2009.
The new voice is part of its "biggest navigation upgrade in over a decade," Google explained in March, part of which includes more "natural directions."

In other words, as opposed to telling you turn left in 500 metres, the app will tell you to "'Go past this light. Then, at the next one, turn left onto Yonge Street,' in the new natural voice," Google told CBC News.

It's not the first time a corporate voice overhaul has triggered backlash. TikTok users hated the new text-to-speech voice when the company changed it in 2021, for instance, airing concerns it was "too excited," "too nice," and having too much "vocal fry."
Last year, iPhone users noticed "Siri doesn’t quite sound like Siri anymore," as Mashable noted. And there was downright outrage when Amazon recently updated its voice assistant, Alexa.

items: TikTok debuts new voice — after Canadian actor sues over the old one
The original voice of Siri still has no clue how she ended up on your iPhones

blocks.text: Some recent studies have suggested people can develop parasocial relationships or dependencies on some product models, especially AI chatbots, and changes to those models can lead to emotional distress.
But social media posts suggest the effect of changing the Google Maps voice may be slightly less deep.
"Why … did my Google Maps voice change to a woman who sounds pissed off???" someone wrote on X this week.
"She sounds mad at me," someone else commented.
The Canadian behind that famous TikTok voice

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. articles.title: Argentina drops investigation into President Milei over crypto fraud
articles.summary: Javier Milei had denied acting fraudulently when a cryptocurrency nosedived after he deleted a social media post about it.

blocks.text: A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped.
The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.
The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra , which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.

He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.
Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category", and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.
Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.
The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.
But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.

It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.
The Argentinian president, though, insisted: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it" in an interview with local media Todo Noticias'.
The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine if the president had acted improperly.
Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".
And, in a TV interview, he insisted that those who invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

articles.title: Conservatives accuse government of 'cooking the books' over immigration data presentation
articles.summary: The federal Conservatives are accusing Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada of exaggerating the decrease in new permanent residents in official messaging posted online.

image.caption: Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner says the federal government is misrepresenting how many permanent residents it is allowing in Canada. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal Conservatives are accusing Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada of exaggerating the decrease in new permanent residents in official messaging posted online.
Critic Michelle Rempel Garner says graph published by IRCC inaccurately depicts immigration numbers
Immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner is calling for better data disclosure following the publication of a graph promoting efforts to restore immigration to sustainable levels.

The graph shows the number of new permanent residents each month since 2023. But starting in 2026, instead of one bar showing the total number of permanent residents, it breaks them into three separate bars.
Rempel Garner says the federal government isn't showing Canadians the full picture.

"They need to reform the system and that includes exit tracking and transparent disclosure of data in a way that isn't designed to fool the (parliamentary) press gallery. Or beat reporters in immigration. Or me, as a parliamentarian," said Rempel Garner.

A graph from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada is being criticized by the federal Conservatives for not accurately depicting the broader picture of people given permanent residence in Canada. (IRCC)
The graphic, as presented, also only goes back to 2023 — a high water mark for permanent residency numbers.
The total number of new permanent residents to Canada in August 2026 is 40,155 — up from 26,080 in December 2025, and higher than some months in 2024.
The same IRCC data visualized with all types of permanent residence programs stacked together, using a longer timeline, shows a different picture.
Comparing year-over-year so far, there are total of 14,155 fewer new permanent residents in Canada in 2026.

IRCC is defending its messaging, saying the image distinguishes people made permanent residents under two one-time programs — and they are not counting those people toward their permanent resident target.
It says the initiatives are temporary for 2026 and 2027.
The one-time programs "provide stability to people who are already in Canada contributing to our economy," said IRCC spokesperson Briannah Dale.
One of those programs is the In-Canada Workers Initiative, which accelerates permanent residence for 33,000 people already working in small communities in in-demand sectors.
The other is for protected persons and their in-Canada dependents to process permanent residence applications from up to 115,000 eligible individuals.
But Rempel Garner says this is equivalent to "cooking the books."
"We're talking about how we restore Canada's consensus for immigration. We have to talk about that and yet they're cooking the books," she said in a news conference on Thursday.
"This is why I addressed the need for better data disclosure as one of our listed demands prior to the [immigration] levels plan being released."
The federal government's goal for permanent residents in 2026 is 380,000, representing a drop of four per cent.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Indiana police officer arrested for using Flock cameras to search wife
articles.summary:
Justin Craig charged with official misconduct and fraud, after searching plates of wife and ‘previous acquaintance’

An Indiana…

blocks.text: An Indiana police officer has been arrested on allegations that he misused Flock cameras hundreds of times in a case involving his wife and a previous acquaintance of hers.

Georgetown police department officer Justin Craig was charged with official misconduct and two counts of fraud. Documents show that he searched his wife’s license plate more than 80 times and that of a “previous acquaintance” of hers nearly 250 times, the news outlet WLKY reported.
The documents say Craig’s searches started in January and continued up to July.
A reporter from the Washington Post triggered the investigation, the documents show, after he called the Georgetown police chief with the tip.

An internal review by the Georgetown police found that the searches Craig conducted on the Flock system were unrelated to any police investigations, and he had intentionally mislabeled those searches to make them appear justified.
The searches had been labeled with subjects including traffic infractions, narcotics, assault/battery, theft and stolen vehicles.

Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans monthly.

Flock, the company behind the tech, provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. Flock says it intends for its technology to aid criminal investigations, but it has come under increasing bipartisan backlash over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing.

There have been multiple reports of police officers across several US states who have allegedly misused or abused the technology. That includes officers who have been accused of using the cameras to stalk former romantic partners and to track down individuals seeking abortions.

The network the cameras feed in to is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose aggressive tactics under the second Trump administration have drawn nationwide criticism.

After Craig’s arrest, his attorney, Matthew Lemme, released the following statement to multiple news outlets: “Flock sells this same technology to cities, homeowners associations, and shopping malls. When public criticism of it came, the response was to put it on the shoulders of individual police officers. The conduct alleged does not violate any law or department policy.”

The statement continued: “If the public or police agencies believe it should, the answer is to write that law or policy. Having that public conversation about privacy and practice is appropriate. Charging officers before it has even started is not. Officer Craig will file a motion to dismiss the charges against him.”

In August, Flock’s CEO announced the company would be taking steps to curb police abuses of its tech by mandating that law enforcement agencies switch on features that could help audit the way individual officers use its tracking capabilities.

articles.title: Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
articles.summary: Ukrainians held alongside the American say they witnessed beatings and sexual humiliation by Russian guards during his detention.

blocks.text: Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.

He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.

"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

articles.title: Embattled Susan Collins announces exemptions for Maine from Trump Canada tariffs
articles.summary:
Republican facing tough re-election battle in state where Trump’s trade war with neighbor has stirred outrage

Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, announced that…

blocks.text: Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, announced that several industries crucial to her state would be exempted from American tariffs on Canada, a notable win for her as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.

In a statement on X, Collins said that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. She added that many of the state’s farmers rely on specialized equipment and materials from across the border that are “unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense”.

“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products, and I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” she wrote.

Collins, who has served in the Senate for nearly 30 years, is running for re-election against Troy Jackson, a Democrat who has served in the Maine state senate and was a former logger. The race is crucial for the Democratic party’s hopes of flipping control of the chamber, and is so far considered a toss-up.

The trade war between Canada and Maine has touched a nerve in the state, which relies heavily on trade with Canada. Many of the industries most entrenched in the state’s history – such as logging, lobstering and fishing – were expected to take a hit after Trump’s tariff announcements this year.

After Trump placed a 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods, which began 22 August, Canada announced its own retaliatory tariffs in response, ranging from 15% to 50% on $20bn worth of American goods. Canada later withdrew its tariffs on American seafood, which helped Maine’s fisheries in particular.

Maine is considered a purple state, and many within the state – including Collins – consider themselves to have an independent streak. Collins has frequently sought to distance herself from Trump, particularly when it comes to his trade policies, and has broken with her party more than any other Republican senator since Trump took office, according to a New York Times analysis of her voting record.
But her efforts to vote against Trump’s policies have rarely succeeded in his second term so far, the analysis found.

Jackson has frequently seized on this line of attack since replacing Graham Platner on the Democratic ticket. At a television debate earlier this month, Jackson also pointed to Collins’s crucial vote to confirm conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh. The court subsequently overturned Roe v Wade.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in his opening statement.

articles.title: Macron condemns racism after one killed in terrorist shooting near Paris
articles.summary:
Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl

Emmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman…

blocks.text: Emmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west of Paris on Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.

Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes, a town west of Paris, on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.
“What happened today ​marks a turning point for our ⁠country; what happened today ​was ​a terrorist ​and racist attack,” ​Macron said.

He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”. He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.

Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said that the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.
Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.

“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”
Rabeh said everyone in France had a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.
Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.

The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines, west of Paris, at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.

The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night. The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable. Rabeh said the man killed was “of African origin” and that another of the wounded was “of north African origin”.

Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.

The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades. The man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.
after newsletter promotion
“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” the interior minister, Laurent Nunez, told reporters from ⁠Yvelines.

The ‌shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France. Last Saturday saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, which left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country. Renewed protests, over teacher shortages and crumbling buildings in high schools as well as the high cost of living, are expected on Saturday.
Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party, is polling highly ahead of next spring’s presidential election when Macron steps down.
After the Trappes attack, Fabien Roussel, a Communist candidate, wrote on social media that the far right was responsible for “racist hatred” in France.
Le Pen condemned what she called the “abject motive of racism” of the “barbaric act”.

articles.title: Stop-motion movie Wildwood is a staggering masterpiece. It's a miracle it exists at all
articles.summary: Sixteen years in the making, stop-motion animation company Laika's Wildwood is its single best movie ever.

image.caption: A scene from the film Wildwood shows Prue McKeel, voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee, in this image released by LAIKA Studios. (Laika Studios)

blocks.text: Entertainment·review
Sixteen years in the making, stop-motion animation company Laika's Wildwood is its single best movie ever.
Company behind Coraline took 16 years to make Wildwood, a stunning achievement of human ingenuity
There are the kinds of movies that switch something in your brain.

Movies that, after watching, make you skip the bus and inexplicably walk 10 kilometres home. Movies that make you stumble through your door, sit down and fumble out a piece of art — even if it's something remedial, unfinished and perhaps even ugly.

Ones that inspire you to make anything: it just needs to exist, because you're suddenly reminded how astounding it is that each and every one of us can perform a legitimate type of magic: artistic creation.

In this case, that spark of inspiration would be Wildwood, the newest dark-fantasy, stop-motion marvel from stop-motion powerhouse Laika. A 16-years in the making animated behemoth from the studio responsible for Coraline, ParaNorman, Tim Burton's Corpse Bride and Kubo and the Two Strings. And given that pedigree, it's perhaps not too surprising to sit up and take notice when the studio puts out what it — and this critic — are touting as its obvious magnum opus.

That is, perhaps, to be expected, given the amount of work and waiting that's gone into Wildwood. Adapted from the 2011 novel of the same name, Laika's film is a passion project from CEO Travis Knight, one that has been in production for nearly the exact amount of time that he's run the company. The end result just so happens to be the longest, most expensive and one of the most ambitious such projects ever attempted. Which is quite a feat, given it is made in a medium already infamous for its time-intensive creation process.
But it is a process that's led to a stunning achievement of human ingenuity, crackling with so much raw beauty that it feels an understatement to call it one of the best animated movies ever made.

Wildwood is so packed with casual displays of complicated artisanal mastery, it makes you stop and stare every time a character casually hops off a rock — given that animation sequence that must have taken weeks to execute — or when a murder of hundreds of jet-black, clay-constructed crows flit through a spellbinding murmuration that fills up the screen, in what feels like a natural phenomenon that couldn't possibly have been rendered by hand.

What's more, throughout the film, all these characters are physically breathing. Their chests are actually rising and falling due to an internal breathing mechanism Laika invented and maintained for the film's entire runtime — just to give it that one added bit of realism.
The visibly obvious effort it took to make all of these seemingly impossible scenes is the point; a not so subtle jab at generative AI that runs through both the medium and the narrative.

That is even as its story — of a young Prue (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee) and her reluctant friend Curtis (the scene-stealing endearing Jacob Tremblay) travelling through a fantastical forest to save her kidnapped baby brother from magical kingdoms on the brink of war — doesn’t exactly sound all that original.

items: Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes
Tom Cruise is fantastic in Digger. You might hate it

blocks.text: Because to believe some critics, if you’ve seen one Spiderwick Chronicles — or Labyrinth, Bridge to Terabithia, Where the Wild Things Are and on and on — you’ve seen 'em all.

That exact complaint — that Wildwood's done-to-death storyline is its weakest aspect — is already an established critique. This is even as its technical mastery is hailed: a reported $100 million US, more than 200 unique puppets, more than 1,000 artisans and one particularly jaw-dropping battle scene.

That last epic sequence utilizes 3,000 characters across a 12-minute runtime — and its sets, if laid end to end, would be taller than a small building. According to Laika, it required one worker whose entire job was tracking the evolving facial scars of the main character — just for that one scene alone.
Brendan the Bandit King, voiced by Mahershala Ali, appears in a scene with Prue. (Laika)

But according to some early watchers, Knight only afforded those resources for the — admittedly astounding — visuals, effectively sinking all the money into ingenuously crafted internal skeletons, functioning under-skin bicep muscles and fully articulated horses. And then he used the last two pennies to scratch out a script that reads something like Narnia 2: This Time it’s Personal.

Which is strange, given the end result. While it is true Wildwood could have subverted expectations, its stellar execution of the magical kingdom/children-in-peril genre comes together remarkably well. And for its supposed target audience of actual children, there’s a lower chance they've already been embittered by such tropes. More likely, Wildwood will likely become their core memory of such tales.

What's actually the most original aspect of its plot — at least for modern American animated cinema — is a truly shocking level of violence for what is a children's film: guns, swords, death, snarling teeth, blood-curdling threats, arrows in chests and blood trickling from mouths.

Along with the bone-chilling performances of Carey Mulligan as Dowager Governess Alexandra and — especially — Tom Waits as the genuinely terrifying coyote soldier Maksim, it is genuinely surprising how far Knight goes to explore the extremes of terror and emotion that do in fact come along with childhood.

Because now, more than ever, it is genuinely surprising anyone would use so much money to grapple with the realities of how unsettling and terrifying childhood can be. More often, when modern children's entertainment is mixed with true peril, it's released in the walled garden of tax-supported systems: leading Canada's past, uniquely interesting children's programs like Cybersix, The Odyssey or simply deeply disturbing PSAs.

items: Toy Story 5 is the best sequel yet. It's still barely about kids
Elio is Pixar's best, most beautifully brilliant movie in a decade. Too bad it will probably bomb

blocks.text: When brought into modern American contexts, they're expected to ditch the harshness, as Apple TV did for the sunnily sanitized Time Bandits reboot). Or, like some fans already expect will happen to the almost identically terrifying Brothers Lionheart adaptation, the sensible business decision is to instead market dark fantasy as gritty drama to adults.

Which is what makes Wildwood's existence such a singular miracle; it is the result of a particular set of circumstances of its creation — the likes of which are unlikely to happen again. Laika is partially bankrolled by Knight's father, Nike co-founder Phil Knight, and the company's sole money-earning feature remains Coraline. Beyond the labour-, time- and cost-intensive production, every decision in Wildwood — from its alienating animation style, to the specificity of its genre and inherent violence — seems lab-designed to continue that money-losing pattern.

It is a message even cheekily, defiantly shown in the background: "Enjoy handmade art before it's gone forever,” penciled in on a street sign. Its a sort of clarion call for itself; a hidden Easter egg making an argument for a format that can't hope to last long. And, obviously, it's a shot across the bow of generative AI.

But Wildwood also feels designed to do what our current profit-focused system rewards the least: craft something challenging, memorable and aimed away from the lowest common denominator. It feels designed to celebrate human achievement. And it feels designed to celebrate humanity; what we are worth, and what we can do.
Which, of course, is to do magic.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Carney says 'direct casualties' are result of Ukraine's restricted access to Musk's Starshield
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday criticized a decision to restrict Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's military-grade satellite network, saying the move is costing lives.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Istanbul that he struggles 'for the right adjective to describe whoever' restricted Ukraine's access to Starshield. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday criticized a decision to restrict Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's military-grade satellite network, saying the move is costing lives.
PM criticizes 'whoever' decided to limit Ukraine's ability to track Russian strikes

"I search for the right adjective to describe whoever took this decision, or a group of people took this decision, against a country … that is literally fighting for the lives of its citizens against naked aggression," Carney said in Istanbul.
"So are we concerned? Yes, we are concerned."

Early last week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some of their access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, the global satellite communications system owned and operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
Ukraine employs Starshield to both track incoming missiles and jet-powered drones, and to guide interceptor and spy drones, while using Starlink for critical internal communications.
Carney says he is 'concerned' about reported Starlink slowdown in Ukraine

Reuters reported last week that, according to two U.S. officials, the order to restrict the system came from inside the White House. The Wall Street Journal, meanwhile, reported on Wednesday that the restrictions were ordered personally by Musk.

Musk said that Starshield was owned and controlled by the U.S. government, and that any restrictions are decided by the U.S. military and, ultimately, by U.S. President Donald Trump. The commercial Starlink system, he said, was not designed or authorized for military use.
Trump has denied ordering the restrictions. On Friday, Trump said he's unaware of who did, and wouldn't tell even if he knew.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says that since Starshield's capacity had been restricted, his country has been unable to track drones and missiles travelling faster than 160 kilometres per hour.
Ukraine says Starshield not restored
Zelenskyy says those restrictions have complicated Ukraine's efforts to repel Russian missile and jet drone attacks — resulting in the deaths of civilians, including children.

Carney agreed with that assessment, saying it now "does seem clear" the restrictions have "real consequences, human consequences" and that some recent deaths in Ukraine are "direct casualties as a consequence of this reduced ability."

items: Elon, Starlink and the betrayal of Ukraine

blocks.text: "I just refer in the last 36 hours to the attack at the centre of Kyiv," Carney said. "Kyiv, absolutely no dressing up on any sort of military or quasi-military target, just a direct attack on citizens and with immense human suffering. So this is real, this is concrete."
On Thursday, Trump said that Musk has since restored Ukraine's access to the satellite network. But Zelenskyy contradicted that claim in an interview with CNN saying "it still doesn't work."
Ukrainian military officials also said on Friday that the restrictions on Starshield remain in place.
Ukraine’s access to Starlink is still limited, President Zelensky tells me. “It limited our possibility to defend.” https://t.co/eusHc70JO5—amanpour
In an interview with NBC's Meet The Press on Sunday, Zelenskyy was asked directly who he thought was to blame for the Starshield restrictions.

"It’s [the] opinion of our generals, of our government and of course my also opinion … that it was the message from American government to limit this speed, and technically SpaceX did it." Zelenskyy said.
The warning for Canada
The restriction of Starshield comes amid a low point in relations between Kyiv and Washington as Trump seeks to push Ukraine into accepting stronger concessions in a peace deal.
Trump has also been pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, although Starshield is not used on drones conducting those attacks as it does not operate over Russian territory.

items: U.S. envoy Witkoff meets with Putin in Russia amid report Musk throttled Starlink

blocks.text: Without mentioning Trump, Carney said that relying on an ally "that may change their view" puts Canadians at risk.

"Once you realize that, as we have, this government has, it leads to a series of decisions and partnerships that are necessary in order to diversify and to build up sovereign capabilities within Canada or with partners," he said.
Diversifying Canada's defence partnerships, Carney said, will take time "because we're starting from a position where we're highly, highly reliant on certain systems in certain countries."

Zelenskyy is already working to move away from his country's reliance on the U.S. satellite network, signing a letter of intent with Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE on Thursday to develop Ukraine's own satellite communications network.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Russia's attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, are intensifying. DW asked people on the ground what life is like
articles.summary: Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian capital are hitting harder and more frequently, making 2026 one of the long war's bloodiest years for Kyiv. DW asked people on the ground what life is like.

image.caption: Russian attacks have turn Ukraine's capital into a front-line cityImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine. Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city.

With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv, subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls.

"We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months.

blocks.caption: People lie on mattresses in the capital's subway system during the nightImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: 'These sick monsters don't care who they kill'

In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel.
Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time.

"We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said.

blocks.caption: 14-year-old Daniel was killed when an attack hit his building in KyivImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: Danger at home, at school — everywhere

Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day.
"This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone."

"Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks.

In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said.

blocks.caption: Attacks on Kyiv target civilian infrastructure, schools and places where children spend free timeImage: Marina Asmolowa/DW

blocks.text: Kyiv's population persists

Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.

Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter.

Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.

Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.
Russia strikes Ukraine with massive aerial attack
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Loblaw CEO apologizes to 2 million shoppers for personal data hack, offers free credit monitoring
articles.summary: The CEO of Canada’s largest grocery retailer is apologizing to about two million shoppers for a data breach earlier this year.

image.caption: Brampton, Ont.-based Loblaw operates about 2,500 stores nationwide under its namesake Loblaws banner, as well as numerous sub-brands including No Frills, Real Canadian Superstore, Zehrs and Fortinos. (Chris Wattie/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New
The CEO of Canada’s largest grocery retailer is apologizing to about two million shoppers for a data breach earlier this year.
In an email to impacted shoppers, Loblaw CEO Per Bank said: 'We’re sorry for the concern this may cause'

The CEO of Canada's largest grocery retailer is apologizing to about two million shoppers for a data breach earlier this year where hackers accessed private information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, birthdates and purchase details.
Brampton, Ont.-based Loblaw operates about 2,500 stores nationwide under its namesake Loblaws banner, as well as numerous sub-brands including No Frills, Real Canadian Superstore, Zehrs and Fortinos.

In March, Loblaw announced that unauthorized activity took place "in certain Loblaw technology systems" around Feb. 23. In an email this week to impacted customers, the company says its internal investigation found an "unauthorized third party" accessed certain personal information.

"We know you trust us to protect your information, and we take that responsibility seriously," Loblaw CEO Per Bank states in the email seen by CBC News. "We're sorry for the concern this may cause, and are committed to supporting you and helping protect your information."
Loblaw stores returning produce country-of-origin labels after backlash

As a precaution, Loblaw says customers were logged out of applications that use the company's PCiD credentials. These include loyalty programs like PC Optimum, the PC Express online grocery service and the PC Financial portal.
The company is offering two years of free credit monitoring and identity restoration services through TransUnion. Impacted shoppers have until Feb. 28, 2027 to enroll.

items: Save-On-Foods loyalty program members had personal information accessed in cybersecurity breach
Crime Stoppers had 'potentially one of the most harmful data breaches' Canada has seen. What's next?

blocks.text: Loblaw is also advising those who receive the email to "be cautious" about unexpected emails, calls or texts asking for personal information or asking you to click a link or download an attachment.
"Keep an eye on your accounts and report any suspicious activity to the appropriate organization," the CEO says in the email.
Understanding credit monitoring services
Consumers should know that credit monitoring services offer limited protection, warned Cat Coode, a Waterloo, Ont.-based privacy and data strategist.

"It only covers if someone is going to use your information in order to apply for a credit card or apply for certain government documents. It doesn't cover the spectrum of the things that you could do with that data," she told CBC News on Friday.
"The privacy issue can never be resolved … Once your data is available, it is available. ... You can change your credit card number, but you can't change your birthdate."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: James Bond screen tests reportedly happening in London this weekend
articles.summary: Diamonds are forever, but James Bond actors come and go — and the time has come to pick the next 007. Screen tests to choose the star of Amazon MGM's upcoming Bond film are reportedly occurring in…

image.caption: Callum Turner, left, and Jack Lowden, right, are both reportedly in the running to become the next James Bond. (Charles Sykes/Invision/The Associated Press and Richard Shotwell/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Diamonds are forever, but James Bond actors come and go — and the time has come to pick the next 007. Screen tests to choose the star of Amazon MGM's upcoming Bond film are reportedly occurring in London this weekend. Two of the rumoured finalists are Callum Turner and Jack Lowden.
Callum Turner, Jack Lowden reportedly finalists to play the next James Bond
Diamonds are forever, but James Bond actors come and go — and the time has come for a new 007 to take up the mantle.
Screen tests to choose the star for Amazon MGM’s upcoming Bond film are reportedly occurring in London this weekend, according to The Hollywood Reporter and Variety.
Two of the rumoured finalists to become the next Bond are Callum Turner, star of the rom-com One Night Only, and Slow Horses actor Jack Lowden, The Hollywood Reporter said, citing several sources.
No release date has been revealed for the upcoming film, but it will be the 26th official title in the 64-year-old franchise, and the first since 2021.
When asked by CBC if screen tests were occurring this weekend, Amazon declined to comment. In a previous statement, Amazon confirmed that it was already searching for the next Bond.
“While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right,” the May statement reads.

Although the spy’s traditional designation of 007 has been given to other characters before, with Lashana Lynch being the first Black woman 007 in the 2021 film No Time to Die, the role of James Bond himself has not been subject to a casting process since Daniel Craig got the role 20 years ago.
Craig portrayed Bond in five films, starting with 2006’s Casino Royale and ending with No Time to Die.
CBC News has reached out to representatives for Turner and Lowden.
Licence to… cast?

Both men are perhaps currently better known for their famous wives — Turner tied the knot with singer Dua Lipa last spring, and Lowden has been married to actress Saoirse Ronan since 2024 — but landing one of the most-coveted male roles in film history could change that.
Turner and his wife, singer Dua Lipa, arrive at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party in March 2026 in Los Angeles. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)
Turner has previously demurred when asked about Bond rumours.
"I know as much as you do — really, I know as much as you do," he told The Hollywood Reporter in an interview in June.
"I'll tell you what’s so funny about the Bond thing: Even your best friends ask you, people text you that you haven’t spoken to for 10 years — and you know nothing!"

Lowden hasn't commented, but his Slow Horses costar Gary Oldman hinted in an interview with Global News that Lowden was on the short list. Ronan told The Associated Press earlier this month that Lowden potentially being Bond "is not really a subject that's coming up in our house to be honest."

Jack Lowden may be lesser known than his wife, Saoirse Ronan, seen at the Britain Independent Film Awards in December 2024 in London, but that could change if he is cast as James Bond. (Thomas Krych/Invision/The Associated Press)

Josh O’Connor, of Challengers fame, has also been raised as a potential candidate duking it out for the role this weekend. But which actor will have the gravitas to look coolly over the edge of a martini (shaken, not stirred) and say, "The name's Bond. James Bond," remains to be seen.
Dune director to helm film

Canadian Denis Villeneuve, known for the wildly successful Dune franchise, has been tapped to direct the film. Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman are jointly managing the reboot. Pascal said in an interview with Deadline in August that "the end of the year is a good bet," for when we'll know who the new James Bond is.
British screenwriter Steven Knight, creator of the BAFTA-winning television series Peaky Blinders, is writing the script.
Previous casting of Bond films has propelled the careers of lesser known actors. A young Henry Cavill was in the running for Bond in the 2000s before the relatively unknown Craig snagged the role.

Since Craig's turn in the role, there have been calls for the next Bond to be played by a person of colour, but although names such as Damson Idris, Dev Patel and Regé-Jean Page had been floated earlier, that no longer seems to be in the cards.

Producer Barbara Broccoli, who formerly held the rights to the franchise, said in a 2024 interview with The Associated Press that while the next Bond would likely be a man in his 30s, "whiteness is not a given."
Amazon MGM bought out the creative rights for the Bond franchise from the Broccoli family in February 2025.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Trump to exempt some Canadian products from tariffs amid midterm pressure
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is poised to lift tariffs on some Canadian products as Republicans in border states lobby for relief from trade actions that have put them in a shaky political position…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump will soon remove some tariffs on Canadian goods, said Maine Sen. Susan Collins on Friday. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

U.S. President Donald Trump is poised to lift tariffs on some Canadian products as Republicans in border states lobby for relief from trade actions that have put them in a shaky political position ahead of November's midterms.
Maine Sen. Susan Collins says some Canadian goods will soon be exempt from U.S. tariffs

Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins said on Friday that the Trump administration will scrap tariffs on some paper and plastic products, refrigeration and packaging equipment, agricultural machinery and seaweed and algae products, among others, after she relayed how damaging these levies have been for consumers and businesses in her state.

Trump hit these products with a 50 per cent tariff in August, apparently retaliating for Canada's countermeasures on some U.S. goods that were imposed after the president first launched his trade war last year.

"I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner," Collins said in a social media statement announcing the changes.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine, earlier this month. Collins, a Republican, is in a tight race with Democrat Troy Jackson. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Collins, a 30-year veteran of the U.S. upper house, is in a pitched battle for re-election in Maine as she tries to hold off a Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, who has made Trump's trade war with Canada a centrepiece of his campaign.

A moderate Republican who has sparred with Trump in the past, Collins had earlier pressured the administration to drop U.S. tariffs on products like road salt given her wintry state depends on Canadian supplies to keep the roads clear.

Another border state Republican Senate candidate, Michigan's Mike Rogers, has publicly called for an end to the trade war with Canada, saying the tariffs have raised prices at a time when inflation is already high.
Polls show Trump's trade war with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

J.P. Tasker is a journalist in CBC's parliamentary bureau who reports for digital, radio and television. He is also a regular panellist on CBC News Network's Power & Politics. He covers the Conservative Party, Canada-U.S. relations, the Crown in Canada, health policy and the Senate. You can send story ideas and tips to J.P. at jp.tasker@cbc.ca

articles.title: Philippines investigates Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, after child sexual abuse images claims
articles.summary: MANILA/LONDON - Authorities in the Philippines are investigating Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, the wife of Britain's Prince Harry, the Philippine justice undersecretary said on Friday, after…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 2:29am

MANILA/LONDON - Authorities in the Philippines are investigating Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, the wife of Britain's Prince Harry, the Philippine justice undersecretary said on Friday, after allegations he possessed child sexual abuse images.

"Our Anti-Trafficking and Anti-OSAEC (online sexual abuse and exploitation of children) task force in Cebu is currently investigating the matter," Nicholas Ty, Philippine justice undersecretary, told Reuters.
Reuters could not immediately reach Thomas Markle for comment but he was quoted by the Daily Mail newspaper in Britain as saying the allegations against him were untrue and "sick lies".
Meghan, who is American, married King Charles' younger son in 2018. In a statement, she said she was "deeply distressed" over the allegations, first published in Britain's Sun newspaper on Friday.
Markle's son handed evidence to police

Meghan said in her statement that she had known about the allegations against her father, 82, since 2018 and had prevented him from having contact with her children Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, to protect them.

She has been out of contact with her father since the run-up to her 2018 wedding. Days before the event, Thomas Markle said he would not attend due to ill health after he earlier admitted posing for paparazzi pictures.

Philippine interior secretary Jonvic Remulla told Reuters it was Markle's son, Meghan's half-brother, who is also called Thomas, who provided police with evidence of the allegations, including a laptop, confirming details in the Sun newspaper.
Meghan's father, who had lived in Cebu in the Philippines for some time, was now believed to be back in the United States, Remulla added.
Meghan said she was shown a letter which had been sent to British police in 2018 with "troubling and disturbing" allegations about her father, adding that she was told they were being investigated.
British police said they were aware of "media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018."
"We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this," a spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said.
Meghan said she was "deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
"My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children," she said.
The Sun also said Thomas Markle's son had contacted the FBI in the United States over the allegations.

"The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities," the FBI said in a statement. "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."
Harry and Meghan and their children relocated to England in August after living in California for six years. — Reuters

articles.title: Children being exploited by criminals to target Greater Manchester HMOs, police say
articles.summary:
GMP fear vulnerable people being paid to attack buildings suspected of housing immigrants or refugees

Vulnerable people, including children, are being recruited by criminals to damage houses…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England Correspondent

blocks.text: Criminals are recruiting vulnerable people, including children, to damage houses suspected of being HMOs, police in Manchester believe.
In recent weeks, dozens of properties have been targeted across Greater Manchester, mostly in Salford, but also in Stockport and Tameside.

The houses that have been attacked are either HMOs (houses in multiple occupation), or properties that have been mistaken for HMOs. Police have received at least 46 separate reports of criminal damage, with cars also targeted alongside houses.
Windows have been smashed, and walls and doors have been sprayed with graffiti reading “fuck off” and “no HMO”. Houses are being targeted because they are believed to hold immigrants or refugees.
Ch Supt Marcus Noden said: “We suspect vulnerable people are being exploited and paid to damage buildings they believe are HMOs. Some of those being exploited are believed to be children.”

“This recent spate of damage is not being tolerated,” he added. “A 42-year-old man has today been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage at an address in Salford overnight. He remains in our custody for questioning.”

Previously Noden said that officers were “taking this spate of damage extremely seriously and are continuing to relentlessly target offenders, including those who we believe are using and exploiting children to orchestrate the criminality”.
Salford council has also taken down roadside banners that had been put up, which read: “IRLAM AND CADISHEAD SAY NO TO MIGRANT HMOs.”

In a statement, the council said: “We have serious concerns that the impact of the banners is highly likely to spread misinformation, escalate cohesion issues in communities and the potential for inciteful behaviour.”
Police have also said that social media is fuelling the attacks, which began on 5 October, with online platforms being used to “push the message out across different areas”.
Posts with pictures of the damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments, many of them praising the attacks and predicting further violence.
However, some have also been critical of the criminal campaign of damage, including domestic abuse survivors who had recently been housed in HMOs.

Four people have been arrested this week in relation to the attacks. On Monday, a 46-year-old man and a 39-year-old man were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, and on Wednesday a 33-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.
Police have also made previous arrests in relation to the spate of criminal damage, including a 13-year-old boy.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine agree to US-brokered, 1 city ceasefire
articles.summary: The Ukrainian city of Oleshky, occupied by Russia and on the frontline, faces a humanitarian crisis. The localized truce comes as Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said negotiators would meet for wider…

image.caption: Oleshky has faced occupation from Russian forces since the invasion began in February 2022Image: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US first lady Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia in the city of Oleshky, the White House announced Friday. The localized truce, according to the White House, is slated to begin on October 29.
What do we know so far about the ceasefire deal in Oleshky?

The Ukrainian city occupied by Russia on the frontline of the war faces a humanitarian crisis and only around 2,000 people still live there. Prior to the war, the city had a population of around 24,000.
Oleshky has been under blockade since 2025 and was first occupied when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city is located in southern Ukraine, just 9 kilometers (around 5.6 miles) from the major city of Kherson.

"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water," Melania Trump said in a statement. "The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks."
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, thanked the first lady for securing the deal.

"Under our agreement: first a ceasefire will be put in place; second, humanitarian aid will be delivered to Oleshky; and third, civilians will be allowed to move freely out of Oleshky," Lubinets said in a video message posted on Telegram. "The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement."
Russia also confirmed the agreement and said it will halt fire earlier than what the White House announced at 0400 local time (0100 GMT) on October 27.

blocks.caption: Oleshky faces constant attacks, with food and medicine scarceImage: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, residents in Oleshky say Russian occupying forces prevented them from leaving the city. Oleshky residents also say Russia has used civilians to shield military positions in the city — a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Fresh Ukraine talks expected in Abu Dhabi next month
The ceasefire deal in Oleshky comes as US, Ukrainian and Russian negotiators are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi next month to discuss ending the war.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskyy told the US conservative Hudson Institute think tank.
US aims for new round of Russia-Ukraine negotiations

In comments to Russian state news outlet TASS, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also said preparations are underway for a three-way meeting in mid-November. Russian President Vladimir Putin said security would be a main topic for the Abu Dhabi talks.
"That is the security of both countries, Russia and Ukraine, after there has been a transition to a peace settlement," Peskov said.

The Kremlin spokesperson said Russia only sees the Europeans at the table during a later stage in the talks. European leaders such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have said Europe must be involved in future Ukraine peace talks.
"It is clear that the architecture of European security cannot be discussed without other participants," Peskov added.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated at Zelenskyy, and is pressuring him to "make a deal."

Trump has blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices in the US, as the US-Israeli war against Iran has caused the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and drove up the cost of gas at the pump for American consumers.

Trump has backed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to lower prices at fuel pumps, drawing criticism from Ukraine. The Kremlin said Friday that the first tanker of Russian diesel has set sail for the US despite the backlash from Ukraine.
Ukraine still dealing with Starshield issues as Trump defends Musk

Most recently, there has been controversy that tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of the Starshield military communications system that Ukraine relies on, possibly with the backing of Trump.
Trump has denied that he ordered restrictions on Starlink. He also defended Musk in comments to reporters on Friday and said, "Elon will never do anything wrong."
"You know, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump said. "I guess the bottom line, he put it back."
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy and Ukraine said Friday that the system was still being throttled in Ukraine.
"It works, but it's still limited," Zelenskyy told US broadcaster ABC News.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry told AFP news agency and other news outlets that Ukrainians were witnessing "instances of signal loss" when using Starshield.
"There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted," the source added.
